blocks.html: Staying current on AI/ML means drowning in hundreds of clickbait articles a day, which produces FOMO and impostor anxiety and eats time that should go to building. Existing news apps make this worse — they are engineered to always surface something, which is the exact incentive that feeds the anxiety.

And a second problem, learned by shipping the wrong answer to the first. A nightly version of this ran for weeks and worked exactly as designed. It was retired anyway, in its reader's words: “I am not finding this AI news useful as I have to react every time I see a news.” A daily brief optimises for missing nothing, and what it produces is a queue — a queue asks for a reaction each time it grows. Meaning needs a week of material before it can exist at all. So the edition is weekly, and that is the most consequential decision in this document. Reading still runs continuously, because reading is deterministic and nearly free; it is judgement that costs money, and judgement happens once a week.

Kill FOMO, don't feed it. Success is the fewest items you'd regret missing — not the most items covered. The system is explicitly allowed to say "quiet day, go build." Two jobs: (a) be aware and understand why it matters (conversational currency), and (b) get hands-on and understand tradeoffs (weekly homework grounded in your repos).

Five agents on a pipeline, plus an eval and learning subsystem that watches them. Four of the five are pipelines in the strict sense — fixed steps, no tools, a closed world where everything arrives in the prompt. Only the Coach has steps that cannot be written in advance, and it is the only one that gets an agent loop.

blocks.html: Ordered input → process → output. Paths carry a plain description; where a file is a contract between agents, its shape is given.

head: Kind
Path — what it is
Status
rows:
config/profile.json
Who the reader is and what the rules are: role, interests, categories, plus doThisCategory and examplesOnlyForCategories. Injected at run time so nothing personal is hardcoded. Later written by the Tuner.

prompts/framer-prompt.md
The system prompt, verbatim and nothing else. This is the text sent to the model and the text that gets cached.

prompts/framer-contract.md
The I/O contract and hard rules. Documentation — never sent to the model.

data/verified/gatekeeper_<date>.json — the contract between two agents
Shape: date, items[] → id · category · headline · tags · source_excerpt · sources[]. No user_id: the verified pool is shared across readers. source_excerpt is the only text the Framer may draw facts from.

config/scout-sources.md
Scout’s Tier A–D seed source list with reputation priors.

agents/framer.py
Reads all of the above; makes two API calls (write, then grade); verifies quotes; enforces the profile rules in code; computes reading time and counts; writes the brief and appends its spend.

agents/budget.py
Everything that touches money, extracted from framer.py at M1, when Reader becomes its second caller: pricing table, the append-only ledger, month-to-date spend, and reserve_for(calls) / can_afford() — the worst-case bound that decides whether a run may start. Takes a list of planned calls rather than a constant, because Scout's shape is many small calls where the Framer's is one large one.

agents/llm.py
The guard rails around a model call: structured_text(), which exits loudly on a refusal or a response truncated at max_tokens rather than writing a half-object, plus the client factory so .env loading happens in one place. Extracted at M1.

agents/graders.py
The faithfulness family — claim ledger, span verification, the claim-vs-inference test. Moves out of framer.py at M3, when the Coach becomes its second caller.

data/evals/run_evals.py
Regrades a frozen golden case with the current grader, asserts the structural rules, scores usefulness, and exits non-zero on any hard-gate failure.

data/briefs/framer_<date>.json — the Framer’s product
Shape: the verified item fields plus user_id (personalization starts here), generatedBy, readingTimeMin, counts, thread, threadFaithfulness, and per item why · example · connection · ninety · faithfulness, plus _enforcements listing anything code stripped.

data/state/usage.json
Append-only ledger: tokens and estimated cost per call. Read at the start of the next run by the circuit-breaker — this is the cost feedback loop.

data/evals/golden/<date>/
A frozen case: input.json (copy of that day’s verified file), output.json (copy of the brief), labels.json (hand-written verdicts). Copies, never references — so a re-run cannot move the baseline.

blocks.html: Two rows are deliberately both directions — gatekeeper_<date>.json (one agent’s output is the next one’s input) and usage.json (written by a run, read by the next). That is why data/ is organised by lifecycle stage rather than “input” and “output” folders.

blocks.html: The point of the substring test is narrow and worth stating plainly: a model can invent a citation that looks rigorous. Steps 1–3 are all judgment, so a confident mistake is indistinguishable from a correct answer — rows 1 and 2 of the table are identical until code runs. _normalise_text() collapses whitespace and lowercases both sides, so the check survives formatting drift but not invented words. Note the two failures are recorded separately: the claim flips to unsupported (the writing is now suspect) and a grader error is logged (the checker is now suspect). A run can have clean writing and a broken grader, and you want to know which.

Scout and Gatekeeper, merged. They were two agents with one job and a handoff that bought nothing: everything from a URL arriving to a verified item landing in the pool. In: 91 tiered seed domains, feeds where they exist, and every URL you hand it through /add-news. Process: fetch → canonicalise → deduplicate → check provenance and corroboration → store the excerpt, once. Out: the verified pool, and the miss ledger.

blocks.label: Two clocks, and why they are separate

blocks.html:
Reading runs continuously. Publishing runs weekly. That split is the whole cost argument: Reader's work is deterministic — HTTP, string normalisation, set membership — so running it every day costs essentially nothing. Judgement is what costs money, and judgement happens once a week against a pool that has been accumulating.

Triggers, honestly: /add-news fetches on arrival and is the only genuinely event-driven path. Feeds are polled where a domain publishes one, which is the closest thing to an event a newsroom offers. Everything else is crawled weekly. Webhooks effectively do not exist in this space, so the design does not pretend otherwise.

blocks.label: Canonicalisation, and why it gates for free

blocks.html: One URL, one form: force https, lowercase the host, drop a leading www., drop the trailing slash, drop the entire query string. This is code answering a question about code, so it gates at zero cost and can never flake. Its golden set is pairs of URLs that must collapse and pairs that must not — including a planted near-duplicate that differs only by tracking parameters, because a suite of only distinct URLs would be passed by a function that never merges anything.

The interesting claim about Reader is that it gets better as you feed it: every canonical URL you hand over teaches it which neighbourhoods produce items worth having, and it starts finding sources you did not give it. Stated that way it is unfalsifiable, so it is measured instead: of the sources Reader added on its own, what fraction produced an item that cleared the bar? If that number does not rise, the compounding is not happening.

Coverage is the harder direction and is handled honestly rather than solved. The miss ledger records every /add-news URL from a domain Reader did not already hold, and closes the entry when Reader finds that domain by itself. The metric is time-to-close, not count. Unknown unknowns stay unknown — that is the nature of the problem — but a domain you had to hand over twice is a visible failure. Reported, never gated.

The half of the old Digest with no equivalent here, and the sharpest piece of reuse in the pivot. In: the week's verified pool. Process: rank up to ten six-month predictions, re-ranked weekly; collect what named people actually said. Out: the Thought Leadership surface and the resolution ledger.

blocks.label: Quotes: an instruction becomes a check

blocks.html:
The house rule has always been quote, never paraphrase. It was enforced by asking. Asking has now been measured and found insufficient — the Framer's grader was told in plain language, with a worked example, never to enumerate the excerpt's own sentences, and did it anyway in three runs out of five.

So the rule becomes the same substring test the Framer already uses, pointed at a different pair of documents: every quote attributed to a named person must be a literal substring of the excerpt fetched from that source. Free, deterministic, and it cannot be talked out of its answer. A quote discovered through a search index rather than fetched is marked truncated and linked out — a fragment presented as a whole statement is a misquote.

blocks.label: Predictions: three states, and why not two

blocks.html:
Two things about a prediction are checkable the moment it is written, and both gate: it carries a stated falsification condition, and it carries a resolution date. Neither needs a model.

The rest is longitudinal, and the design has one trap in it worth naming. If the system only ever marks Hits, the track record is guaranteed to look good — survivorship bias built into the schema. Avoiding it does not require solving the hard question of whether an unresolved claim will ever come true. The resolution date does it: at the date, a prediction becomes Hit, Miss, or Expired-unresolved. Expired is the honest state for a claim that was not falsifiable enough to score, and it is feedback on prediction quality rather than a guess about the future. A miss is kept and annotated with what the reasoning got wrong. An unscored prediction is a hot take; a scored one is a track record.

Turns the week into practice. In: the week’s briefs + your GitHub repos. Process: pick one or two coherent concepts, design a 60-minute exercise (setup excluded), ground it in a real module or propose a new repo; runs Friday evening / Saturday morning so the expensive repo reasoning is batched. Out: backlog items in data/state/backlog.json. Graded on: code-grounding (assertion-checkable — does the module it names exist?) plus behavioural signals: completion rate, actual time, later reuse. Refactor due here: lift the faithfulness grader out of framer.py into a shared module rather than copying it.

Practice, as the reader meets it. A How it Works sub-tab explains the mechanism. Open Exercises carries one tile per piece of homework, with a gear beside the label for the repository setting — configurable at the start and changeable later, because a system that hard-codes the repo it was born with is a demo. Each tile collapses and holds: a status dropdown (To Start / In Progress / Complete), the learning goal, an estimated duration — sixty minutes or less — and steps detailed enough that pasting one into a fresh chat is sufficient context to continue. A timestamp is written when status moves to In Progress, and actual minutes are recorded at close, optional. Estimated versus actual is the Coach's calibration signal: if actuals run at three times the estimate, the Coach is bad at scoping, and that is measurable rather than felt. It is a diagnostic and never a target — a completion rate you optimise for is a generator that writes easy homework.

Learns your taste. In: signal/noise ratings, homework completions, and explicit “explore X” intent. Process: adjust source reputation and topic priors; assign credit backwards across a delayed pipeline; never act on n=1. Out: updated config/profile.json. Graded on: the slope of every other metric over weeks — it cannot be evaluated on a single run. Guardrails: a diversity floor against echo chambers, and no automated prompt edits — optimising to satisfy your own gate is how a system learns to write vaguer claims and pass.

The front door, and the only agent wired to a live API. In: whatever you do in the UI — a dropped URL, a question, a rating, an intent. Process: classify intent and route (URL → Scout, question → chat over the brief, feedback → Tuner), collate responses, run checks. LLM-routed with deterministic fast-paths: explicit button actions dispatch directly; only ambiguous natural language needs the model. Out: answers to you, and labelled feedback into the eval dataset.

blocks.html: One host, one clock, one store. The system runs on Railway: the web surface, the scheduler and every agent in the same place, with Postgres beside them. That is a smaller change than it sounds and a larger one than it looks.

What hosting dissolves. The predecessor was a scheduled cloud task whose run could not write to its own page — measured, not assumed — so it pushed to email and the page pulled from the email. That entire architecture existed to work around a constraint that does not exist on a host you own. The run writes to the database; the page reads the database. It also puts the gates and the delivery in the same process, which matters more: a faithfulness gate that runs somewhere other than where the writing ships is a gate over nothing.

blocks.html:
The source text is written once, at fetch time, and never re-fetched. This is not a storage preference; it is what makes the faithfulness gate mean anything.

The gate asks whether a quoted span is a literal substring of the source. If the source is re-fetched at grading time, a publisher editing a sentence after publication turns the gate red for a reason that has nothing to do with the writing — and a gate that goes red for reasons outside your control is a gate you learn to ignore. It is the same failure as a model alias moving under a pinned test: the thing you were holding still turns out not to have been held still. Both were found the same way, by a run that should have been reproducible and was not.

A suite built only from known-good inputs can be passed by an agent that does nothing at all — that is not a hypothetical: a grader here reported green for four weeks while failing in both directions, and the case that caught it did so on its first run.

blocks.html:
Two things in that table are worth pausing on.

The Thought Leadership quote gate is the Framer's span check with a different document in front of it. The old house rule was quote, never paraphrase, enforced by asking. This system has now measured what asking is worth: a grader told in plain language, with a worked example, not to enumerate the excerpt's own sentences did exactly that in three runs out of five. The same words, checked in code, cost nothing and cannot be ignored.

Usefulness stops being a guess. It has been printed and never gated because there was nothing to calibrate it against — gating on a metric you do not trust teaches you to ignore gates. The thumbs on the Weekly Digest are the first real labels this system has ever had.

Two grading modes, unchanged: offline regression against a golden set of frozen past material, which is what makes prompt iteration safe; and online production feedback, which is what the thumbs become. The offline half is live — python data/evals/run_evals.py, exit code gates.

Measurement and fixing are kept separate. The Evaluator is a read-only sensor; the Prescriber turns diagnoses into recommended actions; the Tuner is the actuator that recalibrates agents; the Control Room reports and asks you questions, whose answers become new gold labels.

blocks.html: How to read it. Steps 1–4 run in sequence on every invocation of run_evals.py. The fan-out is not a set of scenarios to pick from — it is the whole outcome space, and the column that matters is the last one. Rows 1 and 3 are the two halves of the sentence “the grader works”: row 1 says it does not cry wolf, row 3 says it is still awake. A suite with only row 1 cannot tell a careful grader from a dead one, which is exactly where the harness stands today.

Why the plant must survive Stage 1. The obvious fabrication to plant in negative-01 is the $1.4T one from Stage 1 — and it would be the wrong choice. Its span is invented, so the substring test catches it before Haiku's judgment matters at all, and the case would go green while telling you nothing about the grader. The plant is instead a valid quote with a wrong inference: the source says valued at, the brief says raised, and the span Haiku quotes is genuinely in the text. Only reading comprehension separates them. That is the narrow band where the model is load-bearing, and the only band worth spending a negative case on.

blocks.label: Evals for the Framer — how the gate works

blocks.html: The harness answers one question: “did my last change break something that used to work?” It does that by holding the data still and re-running the current code against it.

items: The yardstick is frozen. data/evals/golden/2026-08-04/ is a copy of one past day — input, output and labels — that never changes. Today’s news flows through data/verified/ and data/briefs/ and never touches it.

What varies between runs is your system, not the data. Same seven items, same labels; only the prompt and code differ. So a red run can only have been caused by your edit — that attribution is the entire point.
It calls the real grader, not a copy: framer.check_faithfulness() is imported and invoked, so what you test is what runs. The stored verdicts in the frozen brief are historical and ignored.
It compares conclusions, not text. Labels match by pattern, so the grader may rephrase a claim freely; what must hold is the verdict.

Three checks: faithfulness (hard gate, ~$0.013) · structural assertions (hard gate, free — DO-THIS scope, example scope, sources, thread, counts recomputed with the Framer’s own functions) · usefulness rubric (soft, ~$0.006).
The output is an exit code. Non-zero blocks the change. A gate that cannot fail is not a gate — which is why the harness is itself tested by deliberately corrupting a copy and confirming it goes red.
Labels grow, never mutate. Every new bug becomes a permanent case; editing an old label to make a red test green deletes your own safety net.

blocks.html: Known gaps, each carried in the Roadmap backlog with the reason it was deferred: the harness regrades the frozen brief, so a change to the Framer’s prompt is never exercised (needs a regenerate mode); flagged claims are surfaced but not regenerated (needs a bounded retry); and the free structural checks don’t run on live days (needs a daily smoke test). Also: every golden unit currently has expected_unsupported: [], so the missed-hallucination path is exercised only by manual negative tests, not automatically.

blocks.html: The techniques this system is built from, and where each one actually lands in the code. Applied means it is running and the named symbol exists; designed means it is specified and not yet written. Every claim below is checkable against the repository.

These concepts are deliberately project-agnostic — they accumulate across everything I build, so the long-form write-ups (one-liner, everyday analogy, diagram, worked code) live in a separate concepts reference rather than inside this repo. This section is the index of which ones this particular system uses, and where.
Eleven techniques. Each names the symbol that implements it, so the claim is checkable against the repository rather than taken on trust.

What it is. Deterministic scaffolding built around a probabilistic model — feeding it, constraining its output, checking it, handling failure — so an unpredictable component produces dependable results.

How it lands here. The output shape is enforced at the API boundary, and a truncated or refused response exits without writing anything rather than leaving a half-built brief that renders fine. FRAMING_SCHEMA, structured_text().
What it is. A JSON schema declared at the call itself, so the model can only emit text that fits the shape you asked for.

How it lands here. No prose is ever parsed and no field is silently renamed; additionalProperties: false stops helpful invention. A required field may be null but never absent, so a missing value is a signal rather than a KeyError. output_config.
What it is. Sending N items in one request rather than N requests.

How it lands here. Cheaper, but mainly a capability requirement: the day's thread draws a line between items, and only something seeing every item at once can write it. Seven separate calls could not produce it. frame_day().
What it is. Caching the fixed prefix of a prompt so repeat calls pay a fraction for it. Stable content must precede volatile content for the prefix to match.

How it lands here. The system prompt is cached; only the changing news is re-charged. Little benefit on a once-daily run, real benefit for the chat surface where calls cluster. cache_control: ephemeral.
What it is. Sending each step to the cheapest model that can do it, rather than the best model to everything.
How it lands here. A large model writes, a small one audits. Beyond cost, a second pair of eyes beats a bigger model marking its own homework. FRAMER_MODEL Opus, CHECK_MODEL Haiku.
What it is. A spend limit enforced before work starts rather than reconciled after it.

How it lands here. Month-to-date spend is read from an append-only ledger and checked against the budget pre-flight. A feedback loop across invocations, mediated by a file. MONTHLY_BUDGET_USD, month_to_date_spend().
What it is. Splitting evaluation into what is objectively checkable — which may block a release — and what is subjective, which is reported only.

How it lands here. Factual grounding and structural rules can fail a run; the quality rubric is printed and ignored. Gating on a metric you do not yet trust teaches you to ignore gates. One gate cuts across the others: grader_errors sits in the same or chain as the label diffs, so an invented citation reddens the suite whatever the labels say — a broken checker is a failure even when the writing is clean. hard_failures → non-zero exit.
What it is. When a model checks another model, the checker is unreliable too — so its evidence must be validated by deterministic code.

How it lands here. The auditor must quote the words supporting each claim, and code confirms that quote is a literal substring of the source. A model can invent a citation; a substring match cannot be talked into agreeing. Seen as an outcome table, it is the only step in the run-time check with no judgment in it: Haiku marking a real claim supported and Haiku marking a fabricated one supported are identical outputs until the substring test separates them. normalise_verdict(), span_found.
What it is. A check that returns different answers on identical input cannot gate anything.

How it lands here. The judge samples at zero. At default sampling it disagreed with itself roughly one run in three, which would have failed builds at random and trained me to ignore the gate. The writer keeps sampling; the judge does not. temperature=0.
What it is. A small frozen set of inputs with hand-written correct answers, re-run on every change to catch what quietly breaks.

How it lands here. One real day, frozen as copies rather than references so a re-run cannot move its own baseline. It grows by accretion — each bug found becomes a permanent case that can never silently return. The set needs one case per direction of failure: a clean day proves the grader does not cry wolf, and a day with a fabrication planted in it proves the grader is still awake. Only the first exists today. data/evals/golden/<date>/.
What it is. Two different checker failures needing two different defences: inventing evidence, versus staying silent about a claim.

How it lands here. Invented evidence is caught by code on every run — the span is not in the source, so the claim is downgraded and a grader error is logged. The mirror failure is invisible by construction: a claim marked unsupported offers no span, so the substring test has nothing to bite on, and an over-cautious refusal looks exactly like a correct one. suspicious_unsupported() raises a warning when a flagged claim's numbers do appear in the source, but it never promotes a verdict. Catching the rest takes a planted case and a label that says find this. check_regression().
Ten more, specified in enough detail to build, each with the phase it arrives in. Kept separate so the gap between designed and running stays visible rather than blurring.
What it is. Feedback cycles built into the system — act, observe, adjust, repeat — with a termination condition, so it self-corrects without a human in the loop.

How it lands here. Today's only loop is a regulator: the cost breaker holds a value in bounds but converges on nothing. The reflection loop that regenerates a flagged item and re-checks it is what turns "flagged" into "fixed". Bounded at one retry — a second failure is the prompt, not luck. Tracked in the Roadmap backlog.
What it is. Separating an agent from its tools across a defined protocol boundary, so either side can change independently.

How it lands here. It does not, and that is worth stating plainly. Nothing in the current plan uses MCP, which makes this the one entry on this page that stays purely theoretical. The natural home is Reader's fetch layer — sources reached through an MCP server rather than bespoke HTTP, which is a small use with a real boundary. Carried in the Roadmap backlog rather than quietly left implied.
What it is. Precision asks how much of what you flagged deserved it; recall asks how much of what deserved flagging you caught. Which you favour is a product decision, not a technical one.

How it lands here. The Gatekeeper deliberately errs toward letting things through: a false negative here is the FOMO this system exists to kill, and unlike a false positive it is invisible. Everything killed is logged so misses stay auditable. M1 — it ships with Reader.
What it is. Checking whether the work you are about to recommend has already been done.

How it lands here. Same repo access as code-grounding, opposite question: grounding asks whether the target exists, reconciliation asks whether the answer already does. Recall-biased — when unsure, offer the exercise with a note rather than suppress it. M3.
What it is. Behaviour is stronger evidence of value than a rating, because people call things interesting that they never act on.

How it lands here. Two signals, arriving at different milestones. M1: thumbs on the Weekly Digest — cheap to give, and the first real label the usefulness rubric can be calibrated against. M3: finishing an exercise, which costs an hour and therefore means more than a rating does. Estimated versus actual minutes is the Coach's own calibration signal. Completion stays a diagnostic and never a target — a completion rate you optimise for is a generator that writes easy homework.
What it is. Attributing an outcome backwards across a delayed, multi-step pipeline to the step actually responsible.

How it lands here. Deferred with the Tuner. When an edition lands badly, the question is which agent caused it — Reader letting a weak item through, the Framer writing it poorly, or the ranking putting it first. A thumbs-down names the symptom, not the cause. This is also where reinforcement learning would live, so deferring the Tuner defers a stated focus area; that is a choice made knowingly rather than discovered later. Later.
What it is. A floor on exploration that stops a personalisation loop collapsing into what you already believe.

How it lands here. Deferred with the Tuner, and it gates the Tuner's recommendations rather than the content: a minimum share of items must sit outside your established priors. Without it, a system that learns your taste converges on agreeing with you, which is the opposite of balancing your thinking with new thinking. Later.
What it is. Deterministic interception points around agent execution, for policy enforcement and observability.

How it lands here. Scheduled for M3, where the Coach runs on the Claude Agent SDK and the hooks come with it: the spend reserve re-checked before every tool call, and a path allowlist enforced as a permission rule rather than asked for in a prompt. Hooks matter there and nowhere earlier for a specific reason — every agent before the Coach is a fixed pipeline with nothing to intercept. M3.
What it is. A test whose input contains a deliberate fault and whose expected answer is find it — the only kind that can fail a checker which has stopped checking.

How it lands here. Every golden unit currently carries expected_unsupported: [], so a grader that approved everything, or had stopped running, would pass the whole suite. golden/negative-01/ closes that. The design rule that falls out of it is easy to get wrong: the planted fault must survive the cheap check. Plant an invented quote and the substring test catches it before judgment matters, so the case goes green while testing nothing. The plant is a valid quote with a wrong inference — source says valued at, brief says raised — which only reading comprehension separates. Carried in the Roadmap backlog as negative-02.
What it is. Telling apart work whose steps are known in advance from work whose steps can only be discovered at run time — and refusing to give the second one's machinery to the first.

How it lands here. Five of the six agents are pipelines: fixed steps, no tools, a closed world where everything arrives in the prompt. The Framer is two API calls in a known order; a planning loop would hand the model the control flow, which is the opposite of what every other concept on this page argues for. It would also destroy the cost bound — the breaker gates on a certain worst case, and a loop's turn count is decided at run time. The Coach is the exception, because searching a repository it has not seen has no writable step list, and it is built on the Claude Agent SDK for exactly that reason. M3.

The through-line. Almost every concept above is a variation on one idea: the guarantee has to come from deterministic code outside the probabilistic system. The schema constrains the shape, the guard catches the truncation, the substring check proves the citation, the frozen labels catch the drift, and zero temperature stops the judge changing its mind. The model supplies judgement; the code supplies certainty. Every place that boundary blurred is a place something broke.

Data is separated from presentation. Agents write JSON to data/; the reader-facing pages render it — Weekly-Digest.html now, with Practice and the Control Hub arriving at their milestones. Files: profile.json (the user profile), YYYY-MM-DD.json (immutable weekly edition record + archive), backlog.json, metrics.json. Every record carries user_id.
Loop / token engineering: the daily path is cheap (small models for Scout/dedup, mid for Framer); the expensive repo-grounded synthesis (Coach) runs only Friday night / Saturday morning.

items: Recall over precision at the Gatekeeper — better a little noise than a missed item (FOMO).
Depth over coverage in homework — one or two coherent exercises, the rest benched to the backlog.
Faithfulness is a hard gate; usefulness is a soft, learned target.
Build for one, don't hardcode one — profile object + user_id seam keep the multi-tenant path open at near-zero cost today.

blocks.html: The brain transfers; the body doesn't. Agent logic is ~80% portable to a product; the local/single-user scaffolding is not. Key economics insight: most of the pipeline is shared — the news is the same for everyone, so run Scout → Gatekeeper once to produce a canonical verified pool, then apply a cheap per-user personalization layer (Framer framing + materiality + Coach) on top. What a product adds: auth + multi-tenant isolation, per-user LLM cost management, per-user cold-start onboarding, and cloud scheduling. Defensibility is the action loop (news → hands-on skill grounded in the user's code) and adaptive personalization — not the news itself.

Treat the system as an experiment: hypotheses (each agent's value), metrics (the evals above), controlled iteration (offline regression before shipping any prompt change), and honest reporting of predicted vs. actual. The append-only Decision Log below is the lab notebook.

decisionLog.lead: The evals reshape around three questions, and a house rule that was being asked for becomes a line of code.
decisionLog.body: The pivot adds two agents whose output cannot be checked the way the Framer's is, so the eval design had to become general rather than Framer-shaped. It sorts into three shapes, and which shape a check belongs to decides whether it may block a build: deterministic (code answers it — free, gates), model-judged against hand labels (cents, gates once the labels cover both directions of failure), and longitudinal (only time answers it — reports first, gates once there is enough history to know what normal looks like). The sharpest reuse in the whole pivot falls out of that sorting. The old Digest's rule for quoting people was quote, never paraphrase, enforced by writing it in a brief. This system has since measured what enforcement-by-instruction is worth: a grader told in plain language, with a worked example, never to enumerate the excerpt's own sentences did exactly that in three runs out of five. So the rule becomes span_found — the substring check the Framer already runs — pointed at a different pair of documents. Every quote attributed to a named person must be a literal substring of the excerpt fetched from that source. Free, deterministic, unarguable. Predictions get three states, not two. Hit, Miss, and Expired-unresolved. Marking only Hits would guarantee the track record looks good, which is survivorship bias written into the schema; but distinguishing not yet from never is genuinely hard and does not need solving. The resolution date does the work: at the date it resolves one of three ways, and expired is the honest label for a claim that was not falsifiable enough to score — feedback on prediction quality rather than a guess about the future. Two things are recorded as not covered, rather than left implied. MCP appears nowhere in the plan, which makes it the only entry in the concepts reference that stays theoretical; its natural home is Reader's fetch layer and it sits in the backlog. And the Tuner — deferred — is the only place reinforcement learning would live, so deferring it defers a stated focus area. Both are choices made knowingly.

decisionLog.lead: Two systems converge into one hosted product; the edition becomes weekly, and Scout and Gatekeeper become Reader.
decisionLog.body: A separate system has been running for weeks — a scheduled cloud task producing a weekly digest, with 91 tiered sources, predictions, drafts and an actual reader. It knows what to say and has no way to prove any of it. This system knows how to prove what it says and has no reader at all. They converge: the Digest's job moves onto this engine, hosted, and the Digest is retired. Weekly, and that is the most consequential decision here. The predecessor ran every weeknight and worked exactly as designed. It was retired anyway, in its reader's words: “I am not finding this AI news useful as I have to react every time I see a news.” A daily brief optimises for missing nothing, and what it produces is a queue; a queue asks for a reaction each time it grows. Monthly is too slow for a field that moves weekly. The two clocks are separate: ingestion runs continuously because it is deterministic and costs almost nothing, while judgement runs weekly because judgement is what costs money. Scout and Gatekeeper merge into Reader. Two agents with one job — everything between a URL arriving and a verified item landing — and a handoff that bought nothing. Hosting dissolves a constraint the old design was built around. That system's run could not write to its own page, measured rather than assumed, so it pushed to email and the page pulled from the email. On a host you own, that entire mechanism is unnecessary: the run writes to the database and the page reads it. More importantly it puts the gates and the delivery in the same process — a faithfulness gate running somewhere other than where the writing ships is a gate over nothing. The old system retires on a criterion, not a date: when M3 has run clean for two to three consecutive weeks. Not feature parity — M2 alone replaces the debrief but not the predictions and drafts, and switching off earlier costs a Friday read for no gain.

decisionLog.lead: The grader stopped crying wolf because it was given less to judge, not because it was asked to judge better.
decisionLog.body: The clean day's 18 false positives are gone — 0 in three runs, identical, with grader errors down from 1 to 0 and the response two fifths shorter. Nothing about the grader changed. What changed is that the Framer now divides every field into fact and interpretation runs, and only the fact runs are put in the payload. Every one of those 18 was an implication, a recommendation or a worked-example scenario; none of them could ever have had evidence, so asking for evidence produced a flag nobody could act on. They are not being judged more leniently — they are not being sent. Scope enforced by the payload, the same move that already excludes headlines. The boundary was measured before it was trusted. Two independent models labelled it blind: 94.6% character agreement on the seven-item day, 96.3% on the planted case, with seven disagreements total, each ruled by hand against the excerpt. A boundary two models find independently is one the Framer can be asked to find at run time; had they agreed 60% of the time this design would have been abandoned for a few cents instead of after building it. The dangerous half is still open, and the honest reading is that nothing has been shown about it. The plant is caught 2 runs in 3 against 2 in 5 before — the same point estimate, a different denominator. The miss is a different failure: the grader enumerating the source's sentences instead of the writing's, which a smaller payload does not touch. What did arrive is a way to see it happen. lifted_claims — a claim quoted verbatim from the source that appears nowhere in the writing — fired zero times in 75 claims on the clean day and fired on the unit carrying the plant exactly when the plant was missed. It reports the behaviour, not the outcome: a lifted verdict can still be right, and one was. So it earns a retry, not a gate — re-deriving a verdict read off the wrong document costs $0.008, while failing a build on it would fail correct runs. No threshold was fitted. Separating 5 lifts from {1, 1} across three runs is a line drawn through three points to make a run go green, which is the failure this whole exercise exists to prevent. The rule ships as any lift retries that unit — the only non-arbitrary form — and only once there are more negative cases to test it against. The fix for the open half is designed and parked in Phase 6: split grading into two calls — the first enumerates claims with the excerpt withheld entirely, the second judges that list against it. The grader lifts from the source because the source is in front of it while it decides what to enumerate; take it away and the failure is not available. Same move as the split itself, one level down. It guarantees the right sentences get judged, not that they get judged correctly — that residual is exactly what negative-01 exists to measure.

decisionLog.lead: The Coach is built on the Claude Agent SDK; every other agent deliberately is not.
decisionLog.body: The SDK runs the agent loop, tool dispatch and context management that power Claude Code, and the question was whether to adopt it across the system. No — for five of the six agents. Scout, Gatekeeper, Framer, Tuner and the eval harness are pipelines: their steps are known before the run starts, they call no tools, and they work in a closed world where every input arrives in the prompt. The SDK's core offer is that the model plans its own steps; this system's core claim, stated in every concept on the Agentic Concepts page, is that the guarantee comes from deterministic code outside the model. Handing the control flow to the model to save writing a five-step function would trade the argument for the convenience. There is a hard cost consequence too: the breaker gates on a certain bound — input tokens plus max_tokens, which the API enforces — and an agent loop has no bound, because its turn count is decided at run time. Yes — for the Coach. It is the first agent whose steps genuinely cannot be written in advance: grounding an exercise means searching a repository it has never seen, and prior-art reconciliation means searching it again for a different answer. Real tool use, a subagent for the second question, and hooks for the spend reserve — all of which the SDK provides and all of which would otherwise be re-implemented worse. The loop gets a second ceiling the other agents do not need: a hard cap on tool-call turns, with the reserve re-checked before each one. Managed Agents was considered and refused — it is for long-running asynchronous work you would rather not host, this is a once-a-day batch job, and it would move the spend ledger and the breaker outside the repo. The general rule, now recorded as its own concept: an agent loop is for work whose steps can only be discovered at run time. Everything else is a pipeline, and should look like one.

decisionLog.lead: The new negative case failed on its first run, and measuring the grader five times per case found it broken in both directions at once.
decisionLog.body: golden/negative-01/ went red immediately, so both golden cases were run five times against the pinned grader to replace guesses with numbers — $0.1131, recorded in data/evals/baseline-2026-09-15.md. On the clean day the grader flags 18 claims it should not, identically in all five runs. Every one is an implication, a recommendation or a worked-example scenario — categories its own system prompt names as never-enumerate. Identical output means this is a systematic refusal to follow an instruction, not variance. On the planted case it catches the fabrication in 2 runs of 5. In the other three it enumerates the source's sentences instead of the writing's and marks everything supported at confidence 1.0 — the scope bug Phase 3 closed, returning on the first case it had never been tested against. Four alternative explanations were ruled out before blaming the grader: model drift (one Haiku 4.5 snapshot exists and the alias never moved — free to check, and it killed the hypothesis before any spend), sampling noise (byte-identical five times at temperature=0), mis-wired inputs (verified in run_evals.py, and confirmed behaviourally: two runs flagged a string that exists only in output.json, so the writing certainly reached the grader), and wrong labels (every flag matches a category the prompt excludes). Both failures are the same failure. Neither is a judgement error — in one the grader is right that no evidence exists, in the other it is right that the source agrees with itself. Both are selection errors, made before any judging: too many sentences from the right document, or sentences from the wrong one. What this says about the suite is the real finding. A golden set made only of clean days can be passed by a grader that flags nothing, so the defect was invisible for four weeks while the gate reported green. One negative case found it on its first run.

decisionLog.lead: A planted fabrication only earns its keep if it survives the cheap check first.
decisionLog.body: Designing golden/negative-01/ surfaced a trap worth recording, because the obvious choice is the wrong one. The natural plant is the $1.4T fabrication already used as the worked example — and it would make a useless test. Its span is invented, so span_found fails and the run-time substring check downgrades the claim before Haiku's judgment matters at all; the case would pass while measuring nothing about the grader. The rule: a negative case must target the narrowest layer that can catch it, not the widest. If deterministic code can catch the fault, the case is testing the code. So the plant is a valid quote with a wrong inference — the source says valued at $965B, the brief says raised $965B, and the span Haiku quotes is genuinely present. The substring test passes it; only reading comprehension separates them. That is the narrow band where the model is load-bearing. negative-01 carries a _note recording why this particular fabrication was chosen, so a later edit cannot quietly swap in an easier one and gut the test. A second negative case follows later for omission — a claim with no source at all, never enumerated — which is the same direction of failure by a different mechanism.

decisionLog.lead: Evals get their own section, ahead of the concepts that reference them; the eval / learning loop folds in as a subsection.
decisionLog.body: The eval material was scattered across three places: the Framer's own subsection carried the terminology and the harness, §6 carried a per-agent measurement table, and §7 carried the loop architecture. Nothing wrong in any of them, but no single place answered how does this actually work. Consolidated into AI Evals, moved to sit directly after Low-level architecture so the mechanism is explained before Agentic Concepts starts citing it. The eval / learning loop becomes its first subsection; the Framer walkthrough becomes the second. Section count drops from twelve to eleven. The split that drove it: the faithfulness check runs at two scales and they were being conflated. Stage 1 — the grader reading the writing, live, every run — stays with the Framer in Low-level architecture, since it is part of how that agent executes. Stage 2 — the harness reading the grader, offline, before a change ships — lives in AI Evals. Each is now drawn as a sequential flow ending in a fan-out that enumerates every outcome rather than illustrating a happy path, because the useful content was always in the branches: three of Stage 1's four outcomes are settled in code, and the fourth is precisely what Stage 2 exists to catch. The “who checks the checker” paragraph was deleted rather than moved — the diagrams say it better than prose did. The framer-evals anchor is kept on the moved heading even though nothing currently links to it — a first pass assumed Plan.json did, and the four hits turned out to be links to prompts/p3-framer-evals.md, a different thing with a similar name. Checking cost a minute; carrying a wrong reason in the record would have cost more.

decisionLog.lead: Term definitions move to a page-level glossary; figures may now be HTML.
decisionLog.body: Two mechanical changes serving one problem. First, the glossary. Technical terms — span, claim, label, grader error — were being redefined at each point of use, and the definitions drifted apart; the word span in particular got explained three different ways before one stuck. Definitions now live once in a glossary map at the top of this file, and any block references one with <span class="gloss" data-term="span">. Restating a definition inline is now a defect, not a style choice. Second, figureHtml. The existing figure block carries raw SVG, whose only tooltip mechanism is <title> — a native OS tooltip, delayed and unstyleable. That was a limitation of the block type, not of the page. figureHtml carries self-contained HTML instead, so a glossed term renders as an italic word with a superscript marker and a styled hover card. Its scoped styles use only the page's existing CSS variables, so the design system can restyle it without touching content. tokens.css still needs a page-wide .gloss rule before glossing works in prose and tables as well as inside figures.

decisionLog.lead: The cost breaker becomes shared plumbing at Phase 4, and changes from stop-after to stop-before.
decisionLog.body: Two findings from walking the Framer step by step. First, the breaker is in the wrong place. It lives inside framer.py; Scout is its second caller. Extract at the second use — not the first, which is premature, and not the third, by which point there are copies to keep in sync. New modules: agents/budget.py for anything touching money and agents/llm.py for the stop-reason guard and client construction. The faithfulness grader follows the same rule later, moving to agents/graders.py when the Coach becomes its second caller. Second, the check is a stop-after. if spent >= MONTHLY_BUDGET_USD tests past spend, so a run starting at $19.95 still completes and lands over budget. The fix needs no prediction: reserve the worst case — input tokens plus max_tokens at the output price — and refuse to start unless it fits. max_tokens is a hard cap the API enforces, so the bound is certain rather than estimated. Simulated on a $20 month: gating on the reserve stops after 181 runs at $19.33, leaving 3.3% unused; today's check runs 188 times and ends at $20.08. The rejected alternative matters as much. Deriving max_tokens from remaining budget was considered and refused: below about $0.08 of headroom the derived cap falls under what the brief needs, so the run pays for a response truncated mid-JSON and writes nothing. That converts a money problem into a correctness problem. Budget-derived ceilings suit degradable output — a list where eight items beats none. This output is atomic: schema-enforced JSON, where half an object is worthless, which the existing stop_reason == "max_tokens" exit already treats as total failure. So: gate on the bound, account on the actual, and never let the budget reach in and reshape the work. When money is genuinely tight the levers are frequency, model choice, or input volume — each of which keeps every run whole.

decisionLog.lead: Practice is the system's revealed-preference loop, and completion rate must never be a target.
decisionLog.body: The signals existed scattered across the spec but the circuit was never described. Naming it: brief item → exercise → I finish, skip or overrun → the Tuner reads the behaviour → tomorrow's brief changes. The asymmetry is the point. A rating on a brief item is stated preference and is weak evidence — people call things interesting they never act on. Finishing an exercise is revealed preference: it cost an hour, and it is the only place this system obtains that class of signal. The skip reason is what makes it actionable — "wrong topic" corrects the Framer's priors, "too big" corrects the Coach's scoping, and without distinguishing them a skip is uninterpretable. New guardrail: if the Tuner optimises completion rate, the Coach learns to generate trivial exercises — completion rises, the product degrades, and the metric reports success throughout. Completion is therefore a diagnostic read only alongside actual-vs-estimated time and code reuse, never an optimisation target. Recorded in metrics.json beside the diversity guardrail. Also: the prior-art verdict is itself gateable — it is answerable against the repo — so it joins code-grounding on the objective axis rather than being taken on trust.

decisionLog.lead: Coach must reconcile against my repos before offering an exercise, not only ground in them.
decisionLog.body: Phase 8 already gives the Coach repo access to verify that the module an exercise targets exists — grounding. The same access answers the opposite question, which was never specified: have I already built this? Assigning an hour of work that is finished in a repo is the fastest way for a recommender to lose trust, and no amount of good writing survives it. Three states: none offers as written, partial narrows the exercise to start from what exists, built retires it and returns a pointer to the code. Recall-biased on purpose, matching the Gatekeeper: a wrong already built silently withholds an exercise I never learn existed — invisible, and precisely the failure mode this system exists to prevent — while a wrong no prior art costs a few minutes and corrects itself the moment I open the repo. When unsure, offer with a note; never suppress.

decisionLog.lead: Repo made public, with the private surface reframed rather than removed.
decisionLog.body: Audited first: .env was never committed and no key literal appears anywhere in history — every blob scanned, not just the current tree, so nothing irreversible was at stake. Two judgement calls followed. profile.json was rewritten as a statement of the reader problem rather than a personal bio — it always was the personalization seam, and framing it that way is both more honest about its role and removes a career-intent line that had no business being public. Control-Hub was kept rather than stripped: its badge and footer read "never publish", which a published page cannot carry, so both were reworded to "private surface · sample data". The surface is still the private one in the design — this instance is publishable only because its numbers are placeholders. Stripping the files would have needed a history rewrite, and the commit history is itself the artifact worth showing. Added an MIT licence, and GitHub Pages so the four HTML surfaces render instead of showing 800KB of bundle source; all seven cross-links between them verified to resolve.

decisionLog.lead: Content/design split adopted for every document — with two classes.
decisionLog.body: All pages become JSON content + a design produced in Claude Design; the JSON is the source of truth and the HTML is never hand-edited. But the two classes need different deliverables. Static docs (Concepts, Plan, System-Design) carry content I maintain, change weekly, and can be regenerated on demand — a finished page is fine. Live surfaces (Signal.html, Control-Hub.html) render agent output that changes daily, so regeneration is impossible: Claude Design must deliver a renderer with a data slot, and the design has to be locked before Phase 6 so the backend can be wired into a fixed template. Locking means freezing the data contract the template reads, not just the visuals. First working example of the pattern: the Knowledge Hub (Agentic_Concepts.json → generated page).

decisionLog.lead: Low-level architecture restructured per agent.
decisionLog.body: One subsection each for Framer (built, in depth) and Scout · Gatekeeper · Coach · Tuner · Orchestrator (designed, one paragraph each: in / process / out / graded on). The Framer's dense internals diagram was replaced with a three-tile inputs → process → outputs flow after it proved hard to read. Module map reordered input → process → output, with the data-contract shapes folded into the path descriptions rather than living in a separate section. Added a side-by-side faithfulness vs usefulness comparison, a terminology table with worked examples (claim, supporting_span, expected_span_contains, false alarm, missed hallucination, omission, grader error, precision, recall), and a plain-language "how the Framer eval gate works" subsection capturing the walkthrough — frozen yardstick, same-function-not-a-copy, conclusions-not-text, and the four known gaps.

decisionLog.lead: Deterministic false-alarm signal added to the grader.
decisionLog.body: When a claim is marked unsupported with no span, Python now scans the claim for numeric tokens (money, percentages, dates) and warns if they appear verbatim in the excerpt — the $965B case, catchable for free. It warns, never promotes: a number's presence says nothing about the claim built on it ("$122B" is in the excerpt; "SoftBank invested $122B" is still false). Proper nouns were dropped from the check — every claim names its own subject, so they fired on fabrications too. This is the only false-alarm signal code can produce: verifying evidence is present is mechanical; verifying it is absent is a semantic judgement Python cannot make.

decisionLog.lead: Three gaps found by walking the design, all deferred to Phase 6.
decisionLog.body: (1) Flagged ≠ fixed — the Framer's faithfulness check surfaces unsupported claims but writes the brief anyway; the reflection loop is one turn, not a retry. (2) No daily check — run_evals.py only runs against frozen golden cases when something changes, so a contract violation on a live day goes unnoticed until the next prompt edit; the free structural checks should run daily as a smoke test. (3) The harness regression-tests the grader, not the writer — it regrades the frozen brief, so a change to the Framer's own prompt is never exercised. Closing that needs an opt-in "regenerate mode" that re-runs the Framer on the golden input before grading (costs one Opus call).

decisionLog.lead: Batching is a default, not a hard requirement — corrected.
decisionLog.body: Framing all items in one call makes cross-item connections free, but a multi-call design is viable: chunk the items, then add an explicit reduce call to write the thread (N+1 calls), accepting weaker per-item connections across chunk boundaries. The real ceiling is output tokens (~60–70 items at the current 24k cap), not context. No dynamic chunking is built, and it may never be needed: the Gatekeeper is supposed to cap volume — a 60-item day means the Gatekeeper failed, not that the Framer needs sharding. Action for Phase 5: add a loud assertion on item count rather than silently truncating.

decisionLog.lead: Added a Low-level architecture section.
decisionLog.body: The page had the architectural why but no implementation depth, so detail lived only in code and commit messages. Now captured: module map with BUILT / DESIGNED status tags, the Framer's 8-step execution order (2 API calls, everything else deterministic), model-routing and cost knobs with observed spend, the raw→framed data contract, grader internals, eval harness structure, and extension points for the next agent. Living section — updated as each agent lands.

decisionLog.lead: Prompt and contract split into separate files.
decisionLog.body: prompts/framer-prompt.md now holds the system prompt and nothing else; prompts/framer-contract.md holds the I/O contract and hard rules. The tell was the marker-extraction regex in framer.py — machinery that existed only to separate two things sharing one file; the loader is now a plain read. Rationale: a prompt-only change shows as a prompt-only diff, and future voice variants map cleanly as N prompt files against one shared contract instead of N duplicated copies. Drift is managed by discipline (change both in the same commit) and by the structural assertions, which already test the contract's rules. Pattern generalises: each agent gets <agent>-prompt.md + <agent>-contract.md in prompts/.

decisionLog.lead: Known limit, carried forward.
decisionLog.body: The gate is deterministic for a fixed input, which is what regression needs, but on unseen days the Haiku grader still occasionally enumerates an inference ("X means Y no longer matters") as a checkable claim. Acceptable while the golden day is fixed; revisit before the grader guards live briefs — most likely by routing it to a stronger model, which is also what the usefulness judge needs before it can gate.

decisionLog.lead: Golden set: frozen copies, and labels that admit uncertainty.
decisionLog.body: data/evals/golden/<date>/ holds input.json + output.json as frozen copies — evaluating the live files would let a Framer re-run silently move the baseline. Labels carry three tiers per unit: expected_unsupported (must flag), tolerated (genuinely borderline under the Framer's own contract — scored neither way, deliberately kept short), and named regression_cases asserted against the claim ledger rather than merely the flag list, so we can demand the grader looked at the $965B clause and found the span. Adding a day is a new directory; the runner globs and needs no edit. A second false positive surfaced during labelling — the 2026-08-13 re-run flagged "~80% of Q1 dollars", which its excerpt states word for word — and is seeded as the second regression case.

decisionLog.lead: Verify the verifier's evidence, in code.
decisionLog.body: Every span the grader quotes is checked as a literal substring of the excerpt; a claim "supported" by a span that isn't there is downgraded to unsupported and recorded as a grader error, gated separately from false positives. A grader can invent a citation; a substring match cannot. Paired with temperature=0 on the grader — at default sampling it disagreed with itself on borderline sentences roughly one run in three, which would have failed builds at random (5/5 clean runs after; fabrication detection unaffected).

decisionLog.lead: Root cause of the $965B false positive: grading scope, not carelessness.
decisionLog.body: The grader was handed source_excerpt first and the framing second, and so enumerated the excerpt's claims and checked them against the excerpt — grading the ground truth against itself. It never read the framing, which is why a supported claim looked unsupported and, as a seeded fabrication test proved, why invented facts passed clean. Fixes: the writing under test comes first in the payload and is named writing_under_test; the excerpt is named ground_truth_excerpt; each claim must be phrased as the writing phrases it and carry a verbatim supporting span before any verdict; headlines are excluded (the Gatekeeper wrote them); and the day-level thread is graded against the union of every excerpt, never one item's. Flag lists are now derived in code from the claim ledger rather than taken as a second free-text field.

decisionLog.lead: Phase 3 done (Opus 5). The Framer grader is now itself under test.
decisionLog.body: data/evals/run_evals.py runs three checks over each frozen golden day: faithfulness (hard gate, one Haiku call — regrades the committed framing and compares to hand labels, reporting false positives and false negatives), structural assertions (hard gate, no API — DO THIS only on AI, worked examples only on allowed categories, sources present, thread non-empty, reading time and counts recomputed with the Framer's own functions), and usefulness (LLM judge on a four-part rubric, printed but not gating until calibrated against real ratings). Non-zero exit gates future prompt changes. ~$0.02 per run, on the same ledger and circuit-breaker as the Framer.

decisionLog.lead: Repo reorganised by role; data named by producing agent.
decisionLog.body: Flat root replaced with agents/ · application/ · config/ · data/ · design/ · plan/ · prompts/. Three principles: (1) config vs data — hand-authored files that rarely change (profile.json, scout-sources.md) live in config/, machine-generated files in data/; (2) no input/output folders — the same file is one agent's output and the next agent's input, so data/ splits by lifecycle (verified/ · briefs/ · state/ · evals/) and each file is prefixed with the agent that wrote it (gatekeeper_YYYY-MM-DD.json → framer_YYYY-MM-DD.json); (3) telemetry is its own tier (data/state/). Retired News-reference.html — application/Signal.html now renders that design live, so the p2 prompt points there instead. All hardcoded paths in agents/framer.py, every doc/prompt reference, and all cross-page links were updated and verified.

decisionLog.lead: Visual design system adopted.
decisionLog.body: All surfaces now share one theme: warm cream #f2ebdc page, #faf5ea cards, rust-terracotta #b5502a accent, forest green #2f6b52 for positive/DO THIS, Newsreader serif headlines + Public Sans body. Applied to Signal, System-Design, Plan, Control-Hub, and the Knowledge Hub concepts reference. Architecture diagrams stay on dark cards for legibility on the light page.

decisionLog.lead: Surfaces split by lifecycle.
decisionLog.body: The combined Signal page became two single-purpose files: Signal.html (the daily News brief — regenerated by the Framer) and System-Design.html (this living design record — hand-updated each session). Rationale: the two have different update rhythms, and a compiled/bundled design page can't be hand-edited, which broke the decision-log ritual. Both stay editable plain HTML so the design and maintainability coexist. Cross-references updated in CONVENTIONS.md, Plan.html, README, and the Framer docs.

decisionLog.lead: New agent: Orchestrator (front door).
decisionLog.body: Merges the original Interactive + Feedback agents. Sits between the UI and the agents: classifies user intent, routes (add-source → Scout, question → chat, feedback / "explore X" → Tuner), collates responses, runs checks, surfaces results. LLM-routed with deterministic fast-paths — explicit UI actions dispatch directly; the LLM handles only ambiguous natural-language input. It's the single live-API agent in front of the otherwise-batch pipeline (this bounds the hosting/backend work). Lands ~Phase 9; its v0 is the chatbot.

decisionLog.lead: Infrastructure trajectory.
decisionLog.body: Data: JSON files now → SQLite when history/queries get awkward (at M1) → Postgres + pgvector (incl. auth sessions) at multi-tenant (Phase 11); the user_id seam keeps the migration mechanical. Observability: extend usage.json into a structured per-run trace now → an LLM-observability tool at deploy (~Phase 6+); it overlaps the eval subsystem and feeds the Control Room. Cost tracker: the usage.json ledger + cost circuit-breaker exist now; the Control Room charts it live in Phase 9.

decisionLog.body: The faithfulness check produced a false positive (missed a clause; graded the thread against a single item's excerpt). Decision: the grader needs its own eval, and the thread is checked against the union of all excerpts — Phase 3's first golden-set case.

decisionLog.body: North star = kill FOMO, not maximize coverage; system may declare a quiet day.

claim.def: One checkable statement lifted out of the brief, phrased as the brief phrased it. "Anthropic is valued at $965B"

span.def: Words Haiku copies out of the news text as proof the claim holds. Haiku produces this text, which is exactly why it can be made up.

supported.def: The grader's verdict on one claim. Advisory: code overrules it to false when the span is not a literal substring of the news.

grader-error.def: The grader quoted a span that is not in the news — an invented citation. Tracked apart from unsupported claims, because it means the checker misbehaved rather than the writer. Both block the run.

frozen.def: Sources and writing saved once and never edited — the golden case. Same input every time, so any change in the verdict is the grader changing, not the news.

label.def: labels.json, written by hand after reading the sources. The answer key. A model cannot write it, or the thing under test is grading itself.

false-positive.def: The grader flagged a claim the label says is fine. Costs you good writing, and trains you to ignore the gate.

false-negative.def: The grader missed something the label says is wrong. The dangerous direction: nothing downstream catches it and the fabrication ships.

phase-4-reserve.def: Reserve the worst case — input tokens plus max_tokens at the output price — and refuse to start unless it fits. No prediction needed, because max_tokens is a hard cap the API enforces.

scout.def: The ingester. Merged into Reader at the pivot — it and the Gatekeeper were two agents with one job and a handoff that bought nothing. The name survives in file names and in the decision log, where it describes what was actually true at the time.

gatekeeper.def: The filter: provenance, corroboration, dedup, and the headlines. Merged into Reader at the pivot. Recall-biased — a false negative is a story you never see. The name survives where it describes history or a file that still carries it.

framer.def: The writer. Turns a verified day into the brief: why each item matters, a worked example, the connection between items, and the day's thread. The only agent built so far.

coach.def: Turns the week's briefs into practice — exercises grounded in your own repository. Designed, not yet built.

tuner.def: Learns your taste from ratings and completions, and recalibrates the other agents. Graded on trend, not level. Designed, not yet built.

orchestrator.def: The front door and the only agent wired to a live API. Designed, not yet built.

thread.def: The one paragraph that ties the whole day together. Graded against the union of every item's excerpt, because it synthesises across all of them.

harness.def: The deterministic scaffolding around a probabilistic model — feeding it, constraining its output, checking it, handling failure. The guarantees come from code outside the model, never from the model.

structured-output.def: A JSON schema enforced at the API boundary, so the model's response has a fixed shape. required means a field may be null but never absent; additionalProperties: false stops invented fields.

batching.def: Sending every item in one call rather than one call per item. Here it is a capability requirement, not just a saving: the thread can only be written by something that has seen the whole day at once.

prompt-caching.def: Reusing the model's processing of the fixed part of a prompt. It matches on prefix, so stable content must physically precede volatile content or nothing caches.

model-routing.def: Using different models for different jobs — Opus writes, Haiku audits. A second pair of eyes is worth more than a bigger model marking its own homework.

cost-breaker.def: A spend check that refuses to start a run that would exceed the monthly budget. Gates on the reserve (input tokens plus max_tokens at the output price), accounts on the actual.

hard-gate.def: A check that may block a change, because its answer is objective. Faithfulness and the structural assertions are hard gates.

soft-gate.def: A check that is reported but never blocks, because its answer is subjective. The usefulness rubric is soft, and stays soft until calibrated against real ratings.

golden-set.def: A frozen set of past inputs with hand-written correct answers, re-run on every change. It grows by accretion; editing an old label to make a red test green deletes the safety net.

regression.def: Re-running frozen cases to catch what quietly breaks. The question it answers is narrow and precise: did my last change break something that used to work?

precision.def: Of everything the grader flagged, how much deserved it. Falls when the grader cries wolf.

recall.def: Of everything that deserved flagging, how much was caught. Only measurable where labels exist.

false-alarm.def: A claim flagged as unsupported that the source does in fact support. Erodes trust in the gate — and a gate you have learned to ignore is not a gate.

missed-hallucination.def: An invented claim the grader failed to flag. The dangerous direction: nothing downstream catches it, and it reaches the reader.

omission.def: The subset of missed hallucinations where the claim was never enumerated at all. Code cannot see it, because no span was ever offered to check.

claim-ledger.def: The grader's full working: every claim it extracted, the span it quoted for each, and its verdict. Showing the work is what makes the work checkable.

do-this.def: A tag marking the one or two items that carry an action, not just information. Restricted by code to a single category from your profile.

interest-graph.def: The set of sources, topics and people the system watches. Seeded from 91 tiered domains and grown by the canonical URLs you hand it through /add-news.

framer-py.def: The Framer agent: prompt loading, the two API calls, the faithfulness grader, and the spend breaker. The only agent file that exists today.

run-evals.def: The offline harness. Runs three checks over every golden case and exits non-zero if any hard gate fails. Imports the real grader rather than a copy.

input-json.def: A frozen copy of one day's verified items — the news, as the Gatekeeper left it. The ground truth half of a golden case.

output-json.def: A frozen copy of one day's brief — what the Framer wrote. What was said.

labels-json.def: The hand-written answer key for a golden case. What is true. A model cannot write it, or the thing under test is grading itself.

profile-json.def: The reader — the problem being solved, the categories that matter, and the rules the structural checks enforce. The person, not the taste.

usage-json.def: The spend ledger. Every API call is recorded with its phase, so eval spend and production spend can be told apart.

framer-prompt.def: The Framer's system prompt, kept as a file so editing the voice never means editing Python and a prompt change shows as a prompt-only diff.

framer-contract.def: The Framer's I/O contract — what goes in, what comes out, and the rules. Separate from the prompt because a contract is documentation and a prompt is an instruction.

check-faithfulness.def: The grader call. Sends every unit of writing with the ground truth it is entitled to, at temperature=0, and returns a claim ledger.

build-check-payload.def: Assembles what the grader sees. Scope is enforced by what goes in the payload, not only by asking for it — headlines are excluded by never being sent.

span-found.def: The substring test. _normalise_text(span) in truth — the one step in the whole check with no judgement in it.

suspicious-unsupported.def: Warns when a claim marked unsupported contains numbers that are in the source. Warns only, never promotes — a number's presence proves nothing about the sentence built on it.

reader.def: Scout and Gatekeeper merged into one agent. Discovers, fetches, canonicalises, deduplicates and verifies — everything before a human-readable word is written. Mostly deterministic, which is why it can run continuously for almost nothing.

thought-leadership.def: Writes ranked predictions and the leaders section. Its quotes are gated by the same substring check the Framer's spans are — the same code pointed at a different document.

resolution-ledger.def: Every prediction, scored at its resolution date as Hit, Miss or Expired-unresolved. Misses are kept and annotated: a hidden miss makes the track record worthless.

miss-ledger.def: Every /add-news URL from a domain Reader did not already hold, recorded as a miss and closed when Reader finds that domain on its own. The metric is time-to-close, not count.

excerpt-immutability.def: The fetched source text is stored once, at fetch time, and never re-fetched. The faithfulness gate compares a quoted span against it — re-fetch later and a publisher's edit turns the gate red for no reason.

canonicalisation.def: One URL, one form: force https, lowercase the host, drop www., drop the trailing slash, drop the query string. Deterministic, so it gates for free.

verifier.def: When a model checks another model, the checker is unreliable too — so its evidence is validated by deterministic code. A model can invent a citation; a substring match cannot be talked into agreeing.

precision-recall.def: Precision: of everything flagged, how much deserved it. Recall: of everything that deserved flagging, how much was caught. Reader is biased toward recall on purpose — a false negative is a story you never see, and an unwanted item costs you a glance.

revealed-preference.def: What someone does, weighted above what they say. A thumbs-up is cheap; finishing an hour-long exercise is not, which is why completion means more than a rating does.

hooks.def: Deterministic interception points around agent execution — policy and observability. They matter only where there is a loop to intercept, which is why they arrive with the Coach and nowhere earlier.

pipeline-vs-agent.def: Work whose steps are known in advance is a pipeline and should look like one. Only work whose steps can be discovered at run time earns a loop — handing the model the control flow costs you the cost bound and the attribution.
